title: Starting an Adult Day Care in North Dakota: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

html:
Introduction

Starting an Adult Day Care in North Dakota represents a meaningful opportunity to serve seniors and adults needing daytime supervision, social engagement, and therapeutic activities while building a compliant, sustainable care business. These programs are a cornerstone of the state’s long-term services and supports (LTSS) continuum, offering essential respite for family caregivers and promoting independence for participants. Oversight and funding are administered by the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (ND HHS), with reimbursement and program funding for eligible individuals coordinated through the state’s 1915(c) Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) Waiver.

With significant state funding for HCBS programs (totaling $36.8M in FY2023) and established reimbursement rates for both Medicaid and private pay clients, North Dakota offers a structured and regulated market with clear reimbursement pathways. The market is favorable for providers prepared to navigate the specific licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements set forth by the state. Success hinges on delivering high-quality, person-centered care that meets the social, physical, and cognitive needs of participants.

This guide walks you through every step of launching an Adult Day Care in North Dakota, from understanding state regulations and licensing procedures to staffing your center, developing a budget, and preparing for inspections. Whether you are a healthcare professional, an entrepreneur, or a community advocate, this comprehensive overview will provide the roadmap you need to turn your vision into a reality.

Table of Contents

  • Understand North Dakota’s Adult Day Care Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand North Dakota’s Adult Day Care Regulations

Navigating the regulatory landscape is the first and most critical step in opening your center. North Dakota regulates Adult Day Care Services through the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (ND HHS). These programs are officially classified and licensed as a Basic Care Facility under the specific provisions of the North Dakota Administrative Code (NDAC) 33-03-24.1-21. This classification means your program must adhere to a set of rules governing the physical environment, staffing, and service delivery. The ND HHS is responsible for the entire licensing scope, which includes application review, initial and ongoing inspections, and enforcement of all applicable state rules.

For providers who wish to serve clients funded by Medicaid, compliance extends beyond state licensure. You must also enroll as a Qualified Service Provider (QSP) and adhere to the rules of North Dakota’s 1915(c) HCBS Waiver (#0273.R06.00). This federal framework, overseen by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), ensures that services are person-centered and meet federal quality standards. Additionally, all providers must maintain compliance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) to protect participant health information.

The state’s regulatory framework emphasizes participant safety, quality of life, person-centered care planning, and caregiver support. This means your operations, policies, and daily activities must be designed to protect participants, respect their rights, and provide individualized, meaningful engagement. Licenses are typically subject to renewal annually, requiring providers to maintain a constant state of readiness for surveys and reviews.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Once you understand the regulatory foundation, you can define the specific scope and scale of your adult day care center. North Dakota supports multiple models within the Adult Day Care license, allowing you to tailor your services to meet specific community needs.

  • Social Model: This is the most common model, focusing on social interaction, therapeutic recreation, meals, and general supervision. Activities might include arts and crafts, music, group exercise, and community outings. The primary goal is to reduce isolation and provide a safe, engaging environment.
  • Medical/Health Model: This model includes all the elements of the social model but adds skilled services such as medication administration, health monitoring by a licensed nurse, and coordination with participants’ primary care physicians. This is ideal for populations with chronic health conditions.
  • Specialized Care Model: You can also develop a program that specializes in serving a particular population, such as individuals with Alzheimer’s disease or other forms of dementia. This requires specialized staff training, a more secure environment, and activities tailored to cognitive abilities.

Program size, or capacity, is a key decision that impacts your facility needs, staffing plan, and financial projections. In North Dakota, capacity typically ranges from 15 to 60 participants per day. While the state has an average capacity of approximately 54 slots per 10,000 residents aged 65+, demand varies by region. Demand is often strongest in more populated urban and suburban areas like Fargo, Bismarck, Grand Forks, and Minot, where there is a higher concentration of seniors and working families. Conversely, more rural counties may offer entry opportunities with less competition, but you must carefully assess workforce availability and transportation logistics for participants.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Establishing a proper legal and business framework is essential for liability protection and operational success. Most Adult Day Care providers in North Dakota operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC), S-Corporation, or Non-Profit Corporation. Each structure has different implications for taxation, liability, and governance, so consulting with a legal and financial advisor is highly recommended.

To become a licensed provider, you must complete several key administrative steps:

  • Register Your Business: File your articles of incorporation or organization with the North Dakota Secretary of State to formally establish your legal entity.
  • Obtain an EIN: Apply for an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS. This is required for tax purposes and for hiring employees.
  • Secure Insurance: Obtain necessary insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (errors and omissions), and workers’ compensation insurance.
  • Submit a Licensing Application: The core of the process is submitting a complete licensing application to the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (ND HHS). This application package will require detailed information about your business structure, key personnel, program description, policies and procedures, and facility details. The initial licensing fee is approximately $25 per licensed bed/slot.

Licensing timelines can vary based on the completeness of your application, the time required for background checks, and the scheduling of the initial site inspection. Providers should anticipate that the process will generally range from 6 to 12 months from application submission to final license approval.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is your blueprint for success, guiding your financial decisions and operational strategy. It’s also a critical document for securing funding from lenders or investors. Startup costs for an Adult Day Care in North Dakota typically range from $150,000 to $500,000. This wide range depends on whether you are leasing or purchasing a property, the extent of renovations needed, and initial marketing expenses.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by payroll. Staffing represents a significant portion of the budget, typically accounting for 55-65% of total operating costs, especially given the state-mandated 1:6 staff-to-participant ratio. Other major expenses include rent/mortgage, utilities, insurance, food, and program supplies.

Your revenue will be determined by your payer mix and daily census. Typical reimbursement and revenue ranges in North Dakota include:

  • Medicaid (QSP): Approximately $77.25 per half-day session or $74.68 per 10-hour day through the HCBS waiver.
  • Private Pay: Rates are significantly higher, averaging around $191 per day.
  • Annual Revenue Potential: A well-run center can generate between $500,000 and $1,500,000 annually, depending on its licensed capacity and payer mix.

Financial sustainability is achieved through careful management of your census. Providers operating at a target occupancy or utilization of 70-80% can generally achieve healthy 10-15% profit margins. A detailed financial pro forma in your business plan should project your break-even point, which typically occurs within 12 to 18 months of opening.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Your physical location is central to your program’s success and must meet specific state requirements to pass inspection. The facility must be safe, accessible, and conducive to your planned activities. Key facility requirements in North Dakota include:

  • Space per Participant: A minimum of 60 square feet of usable program space per participant, excluding hallways, offices, and storage areas.
  • Accessibility: The facility must be fully compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), including accessible entrances, restrooms, and activity areas.
  • Restrooms: An adequate number of accessible restrooms to accommodate your licensed capacity.
  • Dining Area: A designated area large enough to comfortably seat all participants for meals.
  • Quiet/Private Space: A room or area must be available for participants to rest, receive first aid, or have private conversations.
  • Safety and Code Compliance: The building must meet all local and state fire, building, and zoning codes. This includes having a functional fire alarm system, smoke detectors, and a documented emergency evacuation plan.
  • Security: A secure entry and exit system is crucial to prevent participants, especially those with cognitive impairments, from wandering.

When selecting a location, consider factors beyond the physical building. Proximity to residential areas with a high concentration of seniors, accessibility to major transportation routes, and proximity to referral sources like hospitals and clinics can all contribute to your success.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your staff is the heart of your adult day care. They create the welcoming atmosphere and deliver the quality care that defines your reputation. North Dakota requires a minimum staff-to-participant ratio of 1-to-6, so your hiring plan must align with your projected census. Required roles in a typical center include:

  • Program Director/Administrator: This individual is responsible for the overall management of the center, including licensing compliance, financial oversight, staff supervision, and community outreach.
  • Activity Coordinator: A creative and energetic person who plans, organizes, and leads the daily schedule of therapeutic and social activities tailored to the participants’ abilities and interests.
  • Direct Care Staff (Aides/CNAs): These are the frontline caregivers who provide direct supervision, assist with activities of daily living (ADLs) as needed, and engage participants in activities throughout the day.
  • Registered Nurse (RN) or Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN): Depending on your service model and the health needs of your participants, a nurse may be required on-site or on a consultative basis for health assessments, medication administration, and care coordination.

All staff must undergo thorough background checks before employment. Training requirements are extensive and must be documented for every employee. Initial and ongoing training should cover topics such as First Aid, CPR, dementia care principles, participant rights, abuse and neglect prevention and reporting, and infection control protocols.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Comprehensive, well-documented policies and procedures are the backbone of a compliant and well-run organization. North Dakota requires licensed facilities to have a detailed set of written policies that govern every aspect of operations. These manuals are reviewed during your initial licensing inspection and on an ongoing basis. Your policies must cover, at a minimum:

  • Admissions, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria
  • Participant Rights and Grievance Procedures
  • Medication Management and Administration Protocols
  • Emergency Preparedness and Evacuation Plan
  • Staffing Plans, Job Descriptions, and Training Policies
  • Infection Control and Prevention
  • Care Planning and Service Delivery
  • Incident Reporting

Individual care plans (or service plans) are a critical component of compliance and quality care. For each participant, you must develop a person-centered plan that outlines their specific needs, goals, preferences, and the services your center will provide to meet them. These plans must be developed in collaboration with the participant and their family or legal representative and reviewed and updated regularly as required by North Dakota and federal waiver rules.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Once your center is licensed and ready to operate, you need to attract participants. Unlike many consumer-facing businesses, marketing in this sector is less about public advertising and more about building professional relationships. Your primary referrals will come from trusted sources within the healthcare and senior services community. Successful providers focus on building a network with:

  • Hospital Discharge Planners and Social Workers
  • Geriatric Care Managers
  • Physicians’ Offices, especially Geriatricians and Neurologists
  • Home Health and Home Care Agencies who serve the same population
  • The North Dakota Aging and Disability Resource LINK, the state’s primary entry point for senior services
  • Local Senior Centers, Veterans’ Groups, and Alzheimer’s Association Chapters

Building these relationships requires a proactive, professional outreach strategy. Focus on demonstrating your commitment to compliance, your high-quality staff, and your ability to communicate effectively with other providers. Responsiveness and clear documentation of participant progress and outcomes will make you a preferred partner for referrals.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Receiving your license is the beginning, not the end, of your compliance journey. Oversight is ongoing and includes unannounced inspections and reviews from the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (ND HHS). Surveyors will focus on ensuring you are adhering to all state regulations and the promises made in your policies and procedures.

Common areas of focus during inspections, and therefore common deficiencies, often include:

  • Inadequate or outdated participant care plans.
  • Errors in medication administration records.
  • Failure to maintain the required 1:6 staffing ratio at all times.
  • Incomplete staff training files or missing background checks.
  • Facility safety issues, such as blocked exits or expired fire extinguishers.

To avoid citations, providers must embrace a culture of continuous quality improvement. This means conducting regular self-audits, keeping all documentation audit-ready at all times, and immediately addressing any issues that arise. Staying current on any changes to the NDAC or HCBS waiver rules is essential for long-term success.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How long does it take to open an Adult Day Care in North Dakota?

A: The process, from business planning to receiving your first participant, typically takes 6 to 12 months. This includes securing a location, completing the licensing application with ND HHS, passing inspections, and hiring staff.

Q: What licenses are required to start an Adult Day Care in North Dakota?

A: You need an Adult Day Care Services license, which is issued as a classification under the Basic Care Facility license by the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (ND HHS).

Q: What reimbursement is available for Adult Day Care in North Dakota?

A: Reimbursement comes from multiple sources. The primary public funding is through the North Dakota Medicaid 1915(c) HCBS Waiver, with rates around $77 for a half-day. Private pay is also a significant revenue stream, with daily rates reaching approximately $191. Some participants may also have coverage through long-term care insurance or Veterans’ benefits.

Conclusion

Starting an Adult Day Care in North Dakota is a challenging yet profoundly rewarding venture. It requires careful planning, a deep understanding of state regulations, and a steadfast commitment to operational discipline. The market provides clear pathways for reimbursement and a growing need for services that support both seniors and their family caregivers. Providers who invest in compliance, build a compassionate and well-trained staff, and cultivate strong referral relationships are positioned for long-term success and a meaningful impact on their community.
